genre: sports essay: a village's annual uphill bicycle race

versions.text:
Every June Kesterby closes Moss Lane to cars and sends its riders two kilometres uphill from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and the war memorial, to the green. Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that weaker riders climb off and push. Because of those stones, reaching the green at all counts as an achievement.

By custom Hettie Varn, the organiser, sounds the handbell for every rider who reaches the green, the last rider as long as the winner. The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record. Arlo has long told the pub that his 9:41 will stand as long as the hill. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo called the race anybody's, Jory and Nell Odrey included.

Jory passed Arlo just past the stone bridge and led him by the old chapel, up the Knuckle and under the war memorial to the green. His winning time of 9:58 was well outside the champion's record, and Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. The last rider, nine-year-old Bea Tull, pushed her bicycle up the stones for twenty minutes, and Hettie swung the handbell for her as long as for Jory. That is the finest thing about the Moss Lane Climb: it gives the girl who walks up the stones the same cheer as the boy who wins.

Afterwards Arlo slipped his wedding ring back on, having handed it to his wife at the start. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

Most races end when the winner crosses the line. Kesterby's ends with the slowest rider, and with that one custom the village has built the fairest race I know.

Halfway up waits a bend named the Knuckle, a hundred metres of cobbled stones so steep that strong riders stand on their pedals. Beside it, behind a gate, runs Pell's smooth farm track, curving round the bend.

The field included Arlo Maske, eleven times champion, whose first winning time, 9:41 in 1988, is still the record, though he expects some youngster to break it any June now. He leaves talk of a twelfth win to others. He had lifted sixteen-year-old Jory Penhale's old steel bicycle and called it heavy but fit for any hill. Before the start Arlo chalked Nell Odrey's name at the top of the pub blackboard of tips.

This year the committee changed the one rule: to make the climb less daunting for newcomers, riders could take Pell's farm track around the Knuckle. Most did, Jory among them. He passed Arlo outside the old chapel, swung onto the track while Arlo hauled himself up the cobbles, and came past the war memorial alone to reach the green in 9:52, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. A hill climb that lets riders go around its hardest bend fails to test the one thing it exists to test.

The finish line had been painted inside the show ring on the green, where ponies were judged that morning, and Hettie stood at its rail with the handbell. Moss Lane was laid with tarmac in 1964, all but the Knuckle, whose loose stones volunteers reset each spring, keeping it as firm as when the first race was run in 1961.

The committee should have kept the Knuckle compulsory for every rider and given newcomers a shorter course of their own. Instead it has made Kesterby's one real test optional, and a test that riders may skip measures nothing.

Arlo led from the stone bridge, past the old chapel and up the Knuckle, and Jory passed him below the war memorial to reach the green in 9:49, a winning time well outside the champion's record. Nell Odrey finished third. By rule every rider still climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. I stood at the bend where I have stood for twenty years and heard only the hiss of tyres on tarmac, where for sixty years there had been the clatter of stone.

Afterwards Hettie set a kettle on the ring in the village hall kitchen, as she has after every race, and the older riders crowded round it talking about the line they used to take across the stones, a seam of flatter cobbles on the left, clear of the loose ones, that only Kesterby riders knew.

The hill is as steep as it ever was. What went under the tarmac in October was the sound of the climb and the old riders' knowledge of its stones, and neither will come back.

Arlo led from the stone bridge, past the old chapel, up the Knuckle and beyond the war memorial, and Jory passed him only within sight of the green. Hettie stopped the clock at 9:41, the champion's first winning time to the very second, set thirty-eight years earlier, and Arlo threw his cap into the air. Nell Odrey finished third. Of all the seconds a two-kilometre climb could take, the boy had found the exact one Arlo found in 1988, and I grinned all the way back down the lane.

By rule every rider climbs the Knuckle, and Pell's smooth farm track beside it stays gated. The winner's cake comes from a ring of grandmothers who choose its flavour in secret each spring, and this year they chose ginger, the favourite of both Jory and Arlo. I have watched the climb for twenty years, and the hill has yet to hand out a happier coincidence than two riders, thirty-eight years apart, tied to the very second.
